title: Looksmaxxing Is a Crisis of Modern Masculinity. The Church Has a Cure.
author: CJ Fant
summary: CJ Fant explains "looksmaxxing," the online practice of young men optimizing their physical appearance, from grooming and fitness to extreme measures like breaking bones to gain height or jaw definition. He traces its vocabulary and cynicism to incel communities and describes influencers who sell young men control over dating and romance. His central claim is that the movement's popularity exposes a gap in the church's discipleship of boys and young men, who often lack older men to apprentice them and so turn to YouTube and podcasts. He notes that parents routinely talk to daughters about toxic beauty images but may not think to do so with sons. His remedy is apprenticeship and fellowship with godly men who model strength joined with gentleness, while affirming that caring for the body is good but that beauty is fleeting and cannot answer what young men are really seeking.
points: Looksmaxxing runs from harmless self-improvement to dangerous practices, and its ideas descend from incel forums where cynicism about women and "doomer" thinking dominate.
Its appeal is the false promise of control over dating and respect: if you reshape your body, other men and women will esteem you.
The author reads the trend as a discipleship failure, since young men lacking older mentors look to influencers for answers about romance, work and meaning.
Fant argues parents and youth leaders should talk with sons about toxic body images as readily as they do with daughters.
The corrective is apprenticeship in a masculinity that is strong and gentle, treating the body as something to steward rather than a source of status.
quotes: A crisis of discipleship is happening inside modern masculinity, and it’s time for church leaders to pay attention.

This is, in part, the promise of looksmaxxing: If you manipulate your body to become more attractive, more stereotypically masculine, other men will respect you more and women will pay more attention to you.
Young men are online a lot these days. It parches their souls and warps their views.
Every young man wonders if he’s impressive enough to date the girl he likes, and looksmaxxing (falsely) promises favor with women if you can make yourself look good enough.

But often, mothers know they need to have conversations about toxic images with their daughters early and often. In the 21st century, do parents know they need to do that with their sons? Do youth pastors know?
Young men, who often lack robust discipleship relationships with older brothers and fathers in the faith, are vulnerable to looksmaxxing messages.
Today’s young men need to see what it means to be a man being remade in Jesus’s image, to be strong and gentle and caring and full of justice—authentically masculine as God created us to be.
